passages.label: Primary inscription: KAI 201 (Melqart stele / Bir-Hadad stele), Aramaic votive text
passages.source_citation: Matthew Saunders (Johns Hopkins University, Dept. of Near Eastern Studies), page "Bir-Hadad Stele (=Melqart Stele; ca. 850-775 BCE; AB B.1.1 = KAI 201)", quoting the Aramaic text and the edition of Jo Ann Hackett and Aren Wilson-Wright 2022, "A Revised Interpretation of the Melqart Stele (KAI 201)", in SAOC 73
passages.source_locator: page sections "Text" (KAI 201 transcription; AB B.1.1; Hackett and Wilson-Wright 2022 vocalized transcription, lines 1–5) and "Translation"
passages.source_excerpt: “The statue which Bir-Hadad, son of ˁAttar-sumkī, Bir-Guš, king of Aram, set up [šm, line 1] for his lord, for Melqart, which he [Bir-Hadad] had vowed to him [Melqart], because he [Melqart] heard his [h, line 5 = Bir-Hadad’s] voice” (Hackett and Wilson-Wright 2022, p. 108).
passages.passage_support: Supports the entry's civic/titular semantics on a primary witness: a named king of Aram addresses Melqart as 'his lord' (lmrʔh lmlqrt) and honours a personal vow; the divine name mlqrt is attested epigraphically. Also gives the stele's date bracket used below (Saunders: late 9th or early 8th c. BCE; Hackett–Wilson-Wright assign 790–760 BCE). Does NOT support Tyrian civic institutions directly: the text is Aramaic and was erected in an Aramaic context (see WiBiLex passage, same caution).
passages.note: The Aramaic line-by-line transcription and the vocalized transliteration are displayed on the page; the translation quoted is the page's quotation of Hackett and Wilson-Wright 2022, p. 108. The page's author states he refrains from his own translation/interpretation pending further study.

passages.label: Primary inscription: KAI 47 / CIS I 122 / IG XIV 600, Cippe de Malte (Phoenician–Greek bilingual votive cippus)
passages.source_citation: Musée du Louvre, Département des Antiquités orientales, collection record "Cippe de Malte" (AO 4818; N III 2298; CIS I 122; IG XIV 600; KAI 47); record last updated 10.07.2025
passages.source_locator: "Inscriptions" field: Phoenician text lines 1–4 and Greek text lines 1–3; "Places and dates" field (Date IIe s. av. J.-C. (selon Ledrain); Place of discovery: Marsaxlokk)
passages.source_excerpt: Inscription du texte phénicien: « 1) A notre Seigneur Milqart, Maître de Tyr, qu'ont dédié 2) ton serviteur 'Abd'osir et son frère 'Osirshamar 3) les deux fils de 'Osirshamar, fils de 'Abdosir, car il a écouté 4) leur voix, qu'il les bénisse » ; Inscription du texte grec: « 1) Dionysos et Sérapion les 2) fils de Sérapion, Tyriens, 3) à Héraklès l'archégète. »
passages.passage_support: Supports the 'civic semantics' leg on a primary bilingual object: the Phoenician dedicatory formula names the god 'Milqart, Maître de Tyr' (b'l sr, 'lord of Tyre' — the same civic formula WiBiLex reports from ~20 inscriptions), and the Greek version renders him as Héraklès l'archégète (founder/archeget) — interpretatio graeca on an institutional dedication. Supports the entry's line-80/82 logic family (translated cult identity, bilingual versions as separate formulations). Date is 2nd c. BCE: late; it cannot be projected back onto Bronze Age Tyre.
passages.note: Record fields are transcribed, not continuous prose. The object is the Louvre cippus; its twin is in the National Museum of Archaeology, Malta.

corroborations.label: tertiary relay with the Phoenician text and transliteration
corroborations.source_locator: "Inscriptions on the Cippi" section: line 1 of the Phoenician text with transliteration and translation; Greek inscription transliteration; "Deciphering the Phoenician script" section
corroborations.source_excerpt: line 1 … lʾdnn lmlqrt bʿl sr ʾš ndr — "To our lord Melqart, Lord of Tyre, dedicated by"
corroborations.note: Gives the Phoenician consonantal text (lʾdnn lmlqrt bʿl sr) with transliteration and the Greek text (Dionysios and Sarapion, sons of Sarapion, Tyrians, to Heracles the founder), and documents the cippi's role in the 18th-c. decipherment (Barthelemy 1758). Confirms that b'l sr appears in the same line as the divine name.

passages.label: Scholarly philological passage: WiBiLex article "Melqart" (Das wissenschaftliche Bibellexikon im Internet / Deutsche Bibelgesellschaft)
passages.source_citation: WiBiLex, "Melqart" (erstellt: Januar 2018), Deutsche Bibelgesellschaft, https://www.die-bibel.de/ressourcen/wibilex/altes-testament/melqart; author line not visible in the retrieved extraction (see limits)
passages.source_locator: §1 "Name und Verortung" (first paragraph); §2 "Schriftliche Zeugnisse" (first and second paragraphs; KAI 47 paragraph; Hannibal treaty paragraph); §4 "Heiligtümer und Kult" (Carthage paragraph)
passages.source_excerpt: “Der Name Melqart müsste nach der phönizischen Schreibung mlqrt eigentlich Milqart vokalisiert werden. Es handelt sich bei ihm um eine Kontraktion von mlk „König“ und qrt „Stadt“. Er bedeutet also „Stadtkönig“.”
passages.passage_support: Direct scholarly statement of the name analysis the entry asserts: contraction of mlk 'king' + qrt 'city' = 'Stadtkönig' ('king of the city'), with the note that the conventional vocalization Melqart should properly be Milqart — matching the entry's hedged 'conventionally Melqart' and 'understood as'. Also supplies: earliest name attestation only to ~800 BCE on the Melqart stele (KAI 201); ~20 Mediterranean inscriptions explicitly link Melqart with Tyre (mlqrt b'l sr, glossed 'König der Stadt, Herr von Tyrus / des Felsens'); the KAI 47 bilinguals naming 'ihrem Herrn Melqart von Tyrus' against Greek 'Herakles, dem Gründer'; Melqart among the oath gods of the Hannibal–Philip V treaty (Polybius 7,9). Profile sentence: “Insofern kann Melqart als Gott der Stadt Tyrus, des (dortigen) Königtums sowie der Erneuerung gelten.” City-variation limit: “Erstaunlich dürftig sind indes die Zeugnisse eines Melqart-Kultus in Karthago” and “Vielleicht passte dieser königliche Heros, Schützer des Königshauses und Archeget auch nicht so recht zu der Geschichte, Entwicklung und dem politischen System in Karthago.”
passages.note: The article's bibliography lists Bonnet, C., Melqart. Cultes et mythes de l'Héraclès Tyrien en Méditerranée (Studia Phoenicia 8), Leuven 1988, and Lipiński 1970/1995 — i.e., the entry's cited authority is a standard reference in this scholarly article's apparatus, but the book itself was not read this round. The article's own caution: the KAI 201 stele was erected in an Aramaic context („diese Stele in aramäischem Kontext aufgestellt worden ist“), so it evidences the god's cross-regional standing rather than Tyrian civic institutions.
passages.language_actually_inspected: German original as retrieved (extraction of the live page); no translation layer.

passages.source_citation: Pamina Fernández Camacho (Universidad de Almería), "Tuna Across the Strait of Gibraltar: Traces of a Lost Fishing Myth?", Euphrosyne 45 (2017), pp. 41–..., open-access PDF in the RODIN repository (Universidad de Cádiz)
passages.source_locator: §2 "Melqart, Heracles: syncretism and myth", opening sentence of the section (p. 44 of the PDF pagination as extracted)
passages.source_excerpt: “The main god worshipped in the city of Tyre was the Semitic god Melqart, a name derived from the roots mlk and qrt (“King of the City”). He had several known facets, such as being the protector of royalty, a solar god, a resurrection god, and later, with the rise of Western colonization, a god of seafaring”
passages.passage_support: Independently (peer-reviewed, not a relay of Lipiński) states the mlk + qrt etymology and 'King of the City'; and gives a multi-facet profile (protector of royalty, solar, resurrection, and later — historically staged — seafaring) that contains no fixed merchant-patron role, matching the entry's refusal to fix the god to one modern occupation. The article's own frame is methodological caution about Greek mediation of Phoenician religion.
passages.note: Quotation copied from the extracted PDF text; the extraction drops some spacing but not wording. The sentence as extracted is cut mid-list ('a god of seafaring and …'); the quotation above stops at a complete word boundary.

basis: All three legs of the tested claim were re-checked against fresh retrievals, primary-first. (1) Name analysis: WiBiLex §1 states the contraction mlk + qrt = "Stadtkönig" and the Milqart vocalization; Euphrosyne 45 states 'derived from the roots mlk and qrt ("King of the City")' — two independent scholarly statements, one encyclopedia and one peer-reviewed article, neither of them a relay of Lipiński's grammar. The designated tertiary page still carries the Lipiński 2002 p. 235 attribution unchanged, so the round-6 relay description of the prior basis remains accurate rather than being displaced. (2) Civic semantics on primary objects: KAI 201, the Aramaic votive stele, addresses 'his lord, for Melqart' (lmrʔh lmlqrt) — a king's votive relation to the god, epigraphically dated to the late 9th/early 8th c. BCE (Saunders; Hackett–Wilson-Wright 790–760; WiBiLex '~800 v. Chr.'); KAI 47 / CIS I 122, the Louvre's Cippe de Malte, carries 'To our lord Milqart, Maître de Tyr' in Phoenician against 'to Héraklès l'archégète' in Greek — the b'l sr civic formula and a translated founder-identity on one 2nd-c.-BCE bilingual. WiBiLex adds that ~20 Mediterranean inscriptions explicitly link Melqart with Tyre. (3) Anti-fixing leg: the retrieved scholarly profiles list multiple roles (city, kingship, renewal, expansion archeget, oath god; protector of royalty, solar, resurrection, seafaring) and WiBiLex documents city variation (sparse Carthage evidence; a royal-hero profile that may not have fitted Carthage), so a single fixed 'patron of merchants' job is not what these sources describe; the trader-protector role appears once, as an Aubet relay inside the tertiary page. The entry's own hedges ('understood as', 'more productive than', named authority) are therefore calibrated correctly; what remains unverified is the book-level attribution to Bonnet 1988 and Lipiński's own page.
limits: 1) Bonnet 1988 (the entry's cited authority) was not read: HAL has a metadata-only record (hal-01853704) with no deposited full text, and the search sweep found no accessible edition. The entry's attribution '(Bonnet 1988)' therefore stays unverified at book level even though its content is consistent with the retrieved scholarly passages. 2) Lipiński 2002, p. 235 was not opened; archive.org's search returned numFound 0 during a session in which archive.org itself reported being temporarily offline, so this is an access limit, not a source verdict. 3) The Melqart stele (KAI 201) is Aramaic and was erected in an Aramaic context (WiBiLex's own caution): it evidences the god's cross-regional standing and the 'lord' votive formula, not Tyrian civic institutions; its date is disputed (Saunders: late 9th/early 8th c. BCE; Hackett–Wilson-Wright: 790–760 BCE; WiBiLex: ~800 BCE) and its royal identity is contested (Albright vs Kitchen vs the Arpad re-analysis), so no single historical setting may be attached to it. 4) The cippus (KAI 47) is 2nd c. BCE and from Malta: its b'l sr formula shows the civic title in use, but the date forbids projecting its institutional setting into earlier Tyre (the entry's line-80 caution applies by analogy). 5) The WiBiLex author could not be named from the retrieved pages (author line not exposed in extraction; grep probe empty). 6) The anti-fixing leg rests partly on calibrated absence across the retrieved source set, which is region- and genre-biased; the Aubet trader-protector relay shows such a function was attested as one role, so the entry must never be tightened into a claim that no commercial role existed. 7) The Euphrosyne quotation is from the extracted PDF text; spacing was normalized by extraction, wording was not.
coupling_implication: Unchanged in direction from round 6, now better grounded: attach Melqart's functions to dated localities and institutions (Tyrian royal cult; KAI 201's Aramaic votive setting; the 2nd-c.-BCE Maltese bilingual as a late translation act), keep the profile multi-role (city god, kingship, renewal, expansion archeget, oath guarantor, and — as one function among others — protector of traders), and treat Greek equivalence (Heracles archegetes) as a diplomatic/translation instrument rather than biography transfer. For fiction systems: a god may be a city's king-god and also a seafarers' patron without either role being the fixed 'real' one; the evidence base changes by city and century.
open_questions: 1) Book-level upgrade: read Bonnet 1988 (Studia Phoenicia 8) directly — the standard reference the entry cites — or at minimum Bonnet's Carthage chapter (pp. 165–201 per the round-8 search hit in a thesis bibliography) to test the 'civic semantics more productive than merchant-patron' argument at source. 2) Re-check melqart.huma-num.fr next round (third attempt) and via Wayback once archive.org is back online; the repertory, if recovered, would carry inscription-level entries. 3) Lipiński 2002 p. 235 remains the one relayed page worth a library/ILL check. 4) If the parent wants the KAI 201 dating tightened, consult Hackett–Wilson-Wright 2022 (SAOC 73, pp. 105–112) directly rather than the relay pages.
